tieu_chi: Nêu ít nhất MỘT điểm giống owl theo bài đọc: tóc white-blond như feathers, mắt nâu nhạt gần vàng, hoặc mũi như beak.

mau: Her white-blond hair flicks around her face like feathers, and her nose is like a beak.

b.a8e3d748.bai_doc:
A Girl Called Owl (Amy Wilson) — Learner’s Book 1.5

When you have a kid, don’t call it something stupid.
Don’t call it Apple or Pear or Mung Bean.
Don’t call it Owl.
This advice is a bit late for me. Because she did. She did call me Owl. Thirteen years ago she looked down at a tiny little baby – me – and decided that Owl would be a good way to go.
I guess she didn’t know then that I would have white-blond hair that flicks around my face, like feathers, no matter what I do with it. That my eyes would turn from baby blue to the palest brown, almost yellow; that my nose would be on the beaky side.
She should have seen that last one coming though; I inherited it from her.
I like owls. I think they’re beautiful, but you know, my head doesn’t rotate 360 degrees. I can’t fly. I don’t hunt at night.
All these are questions the other kids have asked me, over the years. Mum laughs when I tell her.
‘See!’ she cries, looking up from whatever she’s doing, a glint in her dark eyes. ‘Already you stand out in the crowd. Already you are different. Isn’t it a wonderful thing?’
She’s beautiful, my mum. Not in a subjective way, like she’s my mum therefore she must be beautiful. She’s actually beautiful. She has these big dark eyes, masses of dark hair, and when she smiles, when she laughs, it’s difficult not to join in.
I do try my very best not to join in.
Her name is Isolde. She wears lots of bright colours, and tinkling bangles on her wrists. She smells of warm things: vanilla, cinnamon, oranges and blackcurrants, and something deeper that’s just her, I guess.
My friends love her.
Which is annoying.

Part 2
Owl and her friend, Mallory, have just had a maths lesson. Owl was told off by the teacher for sketching owls instead of paying attention.
It was an owl. The doodle in my maths book. I draw them, over and over. Little ones, big ones, owls with crazy whirly eyes, owls swooping down from the sky. They’re in all the borders of my lined school books. They’re on Post-it notes around my bedroom. I have sketches of them, paintings, even little clay figures.
I’m not saying they’re good. Actually, if you walked into my bedroom, you’d probably run back out again, screaming. They’re a bit intense.
Mum loves them. Loves them. She thinks it’s me expressing myself.
Drawing myself, over and over again.
Mallory just rolls her eyes when she sees a new one now. She bought me a card with a puffin on it for my birthday a couple of weeks ago.
‘Maybe a change?’ she wrote inside, ‘Now that you’re thirteen?’
But I’m not called Puffin.
And there had to be a reason.
A reason Mum called me Owl.

tieu_chi: Nêu lý do hợp với bài đọc: Owl vẽ owls mãi, Mallory muốn Owl đổi khác (Maybe a change?).
Nêu được lý do. Nhận trả lời ngắn (cụm từ) nếu đúng ý; không bắt viết câu đầy đủ.
mau: I think she wanted Owl to have a change because Owl draws owls all the time.
Mallory bought it because Owl always draws owls and Mallory thinks she should try a different bird.
b.138bdcf0.bai_doc:
A Girl Called Owl (Amy Wilson) — Learner’s Book 1.5

When you have a kid, don’t call it something stupid.
Don’t call it Apple or Pear or Mung Bean.
Don’t call it Owl.
This advice is a bit late for me. Because she did. She did call me Owl. Thirteen years ago she looked down at a tiny little baby – me – and decided that Owl would be a good way to go.
I guess she didn’t know then that I would have white-blond hair that flicks around my face, like feathers, no matter what I do with it. That my eyes would turn from baby blue to the palest brown, almost yellow; that my nose would be on the beaky side.
She should have seen that last one coming though; I inherited it from her.
I like owls. I think they’re beautiful, but you know, my head doesn’t rotate 360 degrees. I can’t fly. I don’t hunt at night.
All these are questions the other kids have asked me, over the years. Mum laughs when I tell her.
‘See!’ she cries, looking up from whatever she’s doing, a glint in her dark eyes. ‘Already you stand out in the crowd. Already you are different. Isn’t it a wonderful thing?’
She’s beautiful, my mum. Not in a subjective way, like she’s my mum therefore she must be beautiful. She’s actually beautiful. She has these big dark eyes, masses of dark hair, and when she smiles, when she laughs, it’s difficult not to join in.
I do try my very best not to join in.
Her name is Isolde. She wears lots of bright colours, and tinkling bangles on her wrists. She smells of warm things: vanilla, cinnamon, oranges and blackcurrants, and something deeper that’s just her, I guess.
My friends love her.
Which is annoying.

Part 2
Owl and her friend, Mallory, have just had a maths lesson. Owl was told off by the teacher for sketching owls instead of paying attention.
It was an owl. The doodle in my maths book. I draw them, over and over. Little ones, big ones, owls with crazy whirly eyes, owls swooping down from the sky. They’re in all the borders of my lined school books. They’re on Post-it notes around my bedroom. I have sketches of them, paintings, even little clay figures.
I’m not saying they’re good. Actually, if you walked into my bedroom, you’d probably run back out again, screaming. They’re a bit intense.
Mum loves them. Loves them. She thinks it’s me expressing myself.
Drawing myself, over and over again.
Mallory just rolls her eyes when she sees a new one now. She bought me a card with a puffin on it for my birthday a couple of weeks ago.
‘Maybe a change?’ she wrote inside, ‘Now that you’re thirteen?’
But I’m not called Puffin.
And there had to be a reason.
A reason Mum called me Owl.

b.30c10b90.de: Write a short paragraph (4 to 6 sentences) answering the question: "What did you do last weekend?" Requirements: Include at least 3 past tense verbs (regular or irregular), at least 1 negative sentence (e.g., I didn't play...), and sequence words (e.g., First, Next, After that, Finally).

tu_kiem.t: Dài 30–120 từ (khoảng 4–6 câu).
Có ít nhất 3 động từ ở past simple (regular hoặc irregular) viết đúng dạng.
Có ít nhất 1 câu phủ định dùng didn't + V nguyên mẫu (vd I didn't play …).
Dùng sequence words (vd First, Next, After that, Finally) để nối các việc theo thứ tự.
Trả lời đúng câu hỏi: What did you do last weekend?

- Maya: No, I haven’t.

tu_kiem.t: Dài 30–100 từ.
Là hội thoại giữa hai người: mỗi lượt lời có tên người nói và dấu hai chấm.
Dùng present perfect đúng (have / has + V3, auxiliary verb đúng).
Dùng đủ ba adverb: ever, yet, just, đặt đúng vị trí.

b.31b91cba.de: Write a description about a first-time experience you have had. Use interesting nouns and adjectives to describe your feelings. Write sentences in the past simple and present perfect to describe it.

tu_kiem.t: Dài 30–120 từ.
Dùng nouns và adjectives hay để tả cảm xúc (vd terrified, proud, satisfaction).
Có câu ở past simple để kể lại chuyện đã xảy ra.
Có câu ở present perfect để nói về kinh nghiệm cho đến bây giờ.

- big dark eyes
- smiles

tu_kiem.t: Dài 20–80 từ.
Dùng đủ các từ cho sẵn: beautiful, bright colours, big dark eyes, dark hair, smiles, laughs.

Câu hoàn chỉnh, đúng ngữ pháp; có thể nối ý bằng and / but / when cho mạch lạc (gợi ý, không bắt buộc).

b.5840ad4c.de: How do you think you are different to other people? Write a list of the positive things that distinguish you from other people.

tu_kiem.t: Dài 20–80 từ.

Mỗi ý viết đúng ngữ pháp — đề bảo viết list nên câu ngắn hoặc cụm từ đều được (vd I am good at drawing / kind to my friends).
Chỉ nêu điều tích cực về chính em (dùng I / my).

tieu_chi: Viết tiếp vế chính: will / won’t + V nguyên mẫu.
Hợp nghĩa với điều kiện cho sẵn (có thời gian).
mau: If I have time, I will help my mum cook dinner.
If I have time, I’ll read a new book.

mau: Unless you study hard, you won’t pass the test.
Unless you study hard, you will get bad marks.

b.38f1ff3c.t: We will miss the bus, unless we ___.
tieu_chi: Sau unless dùng present simple, thể khẳng định (vd unless we hurry) — không dùng will, không thêm not.
Hợp nghĩa: việc cần làm để KHÔNG lỡ xe buýt.
mau: We will miss the bus, unless we hurry.
We will miss the bus, unless we leave home now.

b.cef485a5.t: If she doesn't eat breakfast, she won’t ___.
tieu_chi: Sau won’t dùng V nguyên mẫu (vd won’t have …).

mau: If she doesn't eat breakfast, she won’t have enough energy in class.
If she doesn't eat breakfast, she won’t be able to concentrate.

The History of Basketball

In December 1891, a gym teacher named James Naismith wanted to find a game his students could play indoors during the cold winters in Massachusetts. He nailed two peach baskets to the balcony railings of the gym and used a soccer ball for the game. Unlike today, the baskets had solid bottoms, so every time a player scored, the referee had to climb a ladder to get the ball back!
As the game grew, people made changes to make it faster and more exciting. In the beginning, there were no backboards, which meant fans in the balcony could reach over and block the shots. Backboards were added to stop this from happening. The soccer ball was eventually replaced by a larger orange ball that was easier to bounce and grip.
In 1946, the Basketball Association of America was formed, which later became the National Basketball Association (NBA) in 1949. This organization helped turn basketball into a professional sport. Today, players like LeBron James and Michael Jordan are famous for their skills, but it all began with a soccer ball and two peach baskets.

Nam was the smallest boy in his class, and the other children often teased him. He loved basketball, but he thought he would never be good enough.
